paper_title: Do Multimodal Models Decide Consistently on Equivalent Optical Spectra?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, $μ$m, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: An optical spectrum can be given as numerical table or plot. Its horizontal axis can show wavelength in nanometers or micrometers, or photon energy. The physical response is the same, but reading and interpreting these forms requires different steps. For example, red shift means longer wavelength and lower photon energy. Also, the lowest point visible in partial spectrum may not be the lowest point in the range asked about. useful decision model should keep its answer under equivalent representations, change it when the question requires different answer, and abstain when necessary evidence is missing. Native decision models receive set of alternatives and return choice with probabilities [3, 18, 26]. This format is convenient for automated scientific workflows. However, valid output format and high average accuracy do not establish whether the model follows the physical meaning of the data or recognizes that part of the required evidence is missing. We test both issues using measured optical spectra and labels calculated directly from the arrays. For each original task, we vary the number format, coordinate, modality, evidence order, question direction, or data coverage. Each change has defined expected answer. To test evidence sufficiency, we compare complete spectrum with two partial views of the same spectrum. Removing data outside the queried interval leaves the answer available. Removing the segment containing the relevant extremum makes the question unanswerable. 1 We then use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [10] to examine which errors an open decision model can learn to correct. The study has three parts: We compare tables in wavelength, micrometers, scientific notation, and photon energy, together with wavelength and energy plots. All use the same underlying arrays. We reverse the question direction to check cases where the answer should change, and vary wording while keeping the energy-coordinate evidence fixed. We remove data inside or outside the queried range of the same spectrum. This tests whether abstention depends on which evidence is missing, rather than simply on whether the input is truncated. We vary the representations, example count, training duration, and answerable truncations used for training. We report all seeds and include controls with similar amount of added data and base model with the same backbone. The largest representation effects occur in energy coordinates. Energy wording helps some modeltask combinations and hurts others. Unadapted models seldom abstain when relevant evidence is missing, and most adaptation gains are limited to the representations and dataset used for training.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Optical response prediction and inverse design. Neural models have also been used to predict spectra from nanostructure geometry. Lin et al. [14] transferred model trained on annular aperture arrays to nanohole arrays to improve prediction with limited target data. Wang et al. [27] used single network to predict transmission spectra for gold nanodisks, truncated cones, and nanocones. Chen et al. [5] combined transmission prediction for annular aperture arrays with geometry search for inverse design. These studies learn mappings between structure and optical response. Our study tests decisions made from measured spectra, including whether the answer changes with the representation or when relevant evidence is missing. Equivalent representations and modality gaps. IsoBench gives the same problems as images, text, and formal notation. It finds that multimodal models generally perform better with text [8]. MaCBench reports similar result for chemistry and materials data, including large text advantage in reading X-ray diffraction peak positions [2]. For some table-reasoning tasks, however, table images match or outperform text formats [7]. Chart robustness studies keep the data fixed and change scale, colour, or layout [17]. We examine coordinate changes that also require physical direction relation, such as longer wavelength and lower photon energy. We include controls where the answer should change and where only the question wording changes. Chart and spectral question answering. ChartQA and ChartQAPro test visual and logical reasoning about charts, with unanswerable questions included in the latter [15, 16]. SpecVQA uses expert questions about seven types of scientific spectra [24]. We use fixed templates and spectra with clear extrema. This makes the comparisons easier to control, but covers narrower range of questions than practical use. Evidence sufficiency and abstention. Whether evidence is sufficient depends on the question. Retrievalaugmented models often answer despite insufficient context. Fine-tuning on sufficiency labels can increase abstention but also reduce the number of correct answers [11]. Easily constructed unanswerable examples can teach cues that fail on harder cases [1], form of shortcut learning [9]. TrustDABench tests refusal when table changes remove necessary evidence, together with invariance under changes that preserve the answer, including unit conversion [25]. In our answerable control, we delete an irrelevant part of the same spectrum. We then test whether adding these examples to training changes abstention behavior. This use of controlled input changes follows the approach of behavioral testing frameworks such as CheckList [21]. Decision interfaces and option bias. Multiple-choice models can prefer particular option identifiers [28]. In typed decision models, option labels can outweigh the definitions supplied by the caller [4]. Effects of thresholds and option order also vary across systems [19], and gains from language-side adaptation may not transfer to other settings [29]. Other work evaluates scientific semantic decisions through their downstream effects [6]. Here Table 1: Evaluation sets. Core variants exist in all six representations; energy-worded probes exist only as eV tables and eV plots. Request counts are for model that supports images. Set Instances Unique spectra Variants Core variants Requests MOCLIP main Gold main MOCLIP scope Gold scope 192 54 54 60 336 70 54 720 244 162 180 528 140 162 180 3,552 1,048 972 1,080 we test evidence order, coordinate meaning, and the queried range. We also compare one decision model with its base model.

sections.title: 3.1 Measured optical data and deterministic labels
sections.content: MOCLIP contains transmission spectra from 10,000 fabricated silicon-on-glass metasurfaces measured under two polarizations [22, 23]. Each spectrum has 29 samples from 450 to 730 nm, spaced by 10 nm. The main evaluation uses polarization. We define the target dip as the global minimum on this grid and do not fit sub-grid minimum. We keep interior dips with prominence of at least 0.15. Their transmission must differ by at least 0.05 from the next local dip with prominence of at least 0.05. Band questions also require 15 nm margin from internal band boundaries. These filters give clear labels and exclude overlapping or unresolved resonances. The second dataset contains 448 peptide-assisted gold-nanoparticle syntheses with measured UVvisible absorbance [12, 13]. Wavelengths run from 300995 nm in 5 nm steps. We use background-subtracted absorbance over 450800 nm, and clean-peak filter keeps 131 spectra. Gold peaks are often broad, so the questions ask which side of threshold contains the maximum. The main threshold is 542.5 nm. We require at least 10 nm separation from it and 3% peak-absorbance margin over the other side. Comparison questions require peak shift of at least 25 nm.

sections.title: 3.2 Task instances, variants, and representations
sections.content: An original instance uses one spectrum, pair, or three candidates. variant changes one part of its question or evidence, and request presents one variant in one representation  (Table 1)  . MOCLIP has four task types, each with 48 original instances. Extreme asks which band contains the minimum or maximum of the same spectrum. Compare asks which of two dips lies at longer or shorter wavelength, with minimum separation of 40 nm. We use both evidence orders and both question directions. Specification asks which of three candidates meets dip-location window and depth threshold. One wrong candidate is deep enough but outside the window; the other is inside but too shallow. The correct candidate rotates through A, B, and C. Sufficiency pairs full spectrum with partial view that removes its true dip. Long-side, short-side, and middle deletions occur equally often. Gold has 20 threshold, 16 compare, and 18 sufficiency instances. Only sufficiency questions offer cannot be determined as an option. We render each core variant as four tables (decimal nm, decimal µm, scientific notation in nm, and eV) and two plots (nm and eV). The conversion is [eV] = 1239.841984/λ [nm]. Transmission and absorbance are response ratios, so changing the horizontal coordinate does not require spectral-density Jacobian. Answer keys are fixed, while the displayed ranges and units follow the representation. Rows in eV tables are sorted by increasing energy, which reverses the wavelength order. Their spacing is nonuniform: 0.060 eV between 450 and 460 nm, and 0.024 eV between 720 and 730 nm. Tables use rounded values. Plots are 800 500 raster images with labeled axes, and middle deletions appear as disconnected segments. The underlying samples and answers are equivalent, but their visual and numerical readability can differ. deterministic program that parses the rendered tables reaches 100% accuracy on every table request. Appendix gives the original requests. Compare questions normally ask about longer or shorter wavelength, even when the evidence uses energy coordinates. Additional variants on eV tables and plots ask about lower or higher photon energy. We use the 3 Figure 1: One MOCLIP scope instance in wavelength and energy coordinates. Shading marks the queried interval and is added for illustration only; model inputs state the interval in the question. same control for gold threshold questions. The evidence stays fixed, so this comparison tests the extra step of relating wavelength wording to an energy axis.

sections.title: 3.3 Query-relative evidence controls
sections.content: Every truncated view in the main sufficiency tasks is unanswerable. model can therefore succeed by treating any missing data as reason to abstain. The scope sets test this possibility. Each question states an interval Q, and each spectrum is shown in three forms: full; with samples outside removed, leaving the answer available; and with the segment inside containing the relevant extremum removed, labeled cannot be determined (Figure 1). MOCLIP uses query intervals of 450685 or 605730 nm. Gold uses 450650 or 490800 nm, with five thresholds from 522.5 to 562.5 nm. Both sets balance long-side, short-side, and middle inside cuts, with 18 MOCLIP and 20 gold instances per type. The MOCLIP scope set uses polarization and excludes all structures used in main testing and training. It reuses some pilot structures because the clean-dip filters limit the available pool. Gold scope and main sets share 30 spectra. They are two task constructions from one dataset, not independent replications.

sections.title: 4.1 Model configurations
sections.content: d3-nano is 2.21B-parameter multimodal decision model fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-2B. We use checkpoint 80820624a817 (v3.1.0 weights) in bfloat16 and its local probability readout [26]. d3-nano-pa averages the runtime outputs for forward and reversed option orders. Jev 1.13 is text-only decision model accessed through OpenRouter [3]. We test three GPT-6 Luna configurations through OpenRouter, with OpenAI as the only provider. These are the decision route (openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions; Luna Decisions) and the generative route through Chat Completions with strict JSON schema at reasoning effort none or low (Luna gen. none, Luna gen. low). The routes share model family and provider. We cannot verify that they share checkpoints or inference implementations, so we compare the available configurations. We did not test the native OpenAI /v1/decisions endpoint [18]. 4 Table 2: Core-variant accuracy (%, 95% instance-bootstrap intervals). MOCLIP has 528 core variants and gold 140. Jev has no image input. The Qwen3.5-2B base row comes from the supplementary batch. sections.title: 4.2 Metrics and uncertainty
sections.content: We calculate accuracy using the canonical answer keys. Unless stated otherwise, summaries of representation, training, and interface effects use core variants. Energy-worded probes are used only in the wording analysis. We measure each representation effect as its paired accuracy difference from the nm table on the same variants. For representation set R, agreement on variant is CR(v) = 1{ ˆyv,r = ˆyv,r r, R}. Higher accuracy also tends to produce higher agreement. We therefore separate agreement into cases where all answers are correct and cases where all are the same but wrong. We compare the all-correct share with its expected value under independent errors across representations, using each representations accuracy within each task type. For the scope sets, with Ui,c,r indicating an undetermined prediction and Ai,c,r correctness for instance i, cut and representation r, Dscope = 100 i,r[Ui,in,r Ui,out,r], out = 100 i,r[Ai,out,r Ai,full,r]. (1) The ideal values are +100 and 0. model that always abstains or never abstains has Dscope = 0. Both measures are relative, so we also report full-view accuracy. The high-confidence error fraction is the proportion of all requests with maxk p(k) 0.9 and an incorrect choice. Generative probabilities are reported by the model in JSON and should not be treated as equivalent to decision-interface probabilities. We calculate 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of original task instances. Each instances variants and representations stay together, and differences are paired within instances. We report LoRA seeds separately. The study developed through sequential pilots, so the intervals are descriptive and have no correction for multiple comparisons.

sections.title: 5.2 Abstention when relevant evidence is missing
sections.content: In the main MOCLIP sufficiency set, we remove middle segment containing the true dip. d3-nano, Jev, and Luna Decisions never answer undetermined in any representation. Low-reasoning Luna abstains on 100% of nm tables, 94% of µm tables, and 62% of scientific-notation tables. It abstains on 0% of eV tables and only 019% of plots. Each cell has 16 instances. The scope sets compare these failures with deletions that leave the question answerable  (Table 7)  . Unadapted API configurations almost never abstain on outside cuts, and their accuracy changes by at most seven points. They also discriminate poorly between inside and outside cuts on MOCLIP. Table discrimination is +14 for Jev, +18 for Luna Decisions, +19 for Luna gen. none, and +55 for low-reasoning Luna. Plot discrimination is at most +16. Base d3-nano never abstains. On gold, Jev, Luna Decisions, and Luna gen. none choose undetermined on only 05% of middle-gap requests. Low-reasoning Luna reaches 2075% on tables and 0% on plots. After an inside cut, common wrong answer is the band containing the visible extremum. Across deletion types in the main MOCLIP sufficiency set, 5481% of d3-nano responses and 3154% of Jev responses select this band, depending on representation. In specification tasks, 75100% of errors select the candidate that is deep enough but outside the required window.

sections.title: 5.3 Adaptation on table tasks and transfer to other settings
sections.content: We adapt only d3-nano. LoRA modules with rank 16, scale 32, and dropout 0.05 are added to the language-model projection layers. The vision tower, backbone weights, readout, and temperature remain frozen. We use AdamW with learning rate 104 and no weight decay, accumulate gradients over eight examples, clip gradients at 1.0, and minimize cross-entropy over the candidate readout. Training uses the evaluation templates, with structures excluded from every test set. It includes neither plots nor specification tasks. hash of the instance identifier assigns about 10% of instances to development  (Table 8)  . Some structures are reused when adding answerable truncations or original-task examples. This leaves 8 structures shared between training and development in ftC 8 Table 8: LoRA arms (three seeds each). Train/Dev count rendered requests. After two epochs on nm tables only, ftA remains at chance on compare, with development accuracy of 0.6750.700. Training the same data to the selected epoch (ftAc) raises development accuracy to 0.9631.000 and compare accuracy on nm tables to 85100%. The two-epoch model was therefore under-trained. Longer training also reduces variation across seeds in the sample-matched four-table arm. Table compare accuracy changes from 63/97/81% for ftBm to 99/94/98% for ftBmc. Representation coverage. ftAc reaches 8299% on µm tables and 7695% on scientific-notation tables, but only 4151% on eV tables (Figure 3). With the same number of examples, the four-table arm ftBmc reaches 94100% on eV tables. This is close to ftB, which uses 4.7 times as many examples and reaches 99100%. In this comparison, including the representation in training matters more for eV transfer than the total example count. The four-table pool also includes energy-worded variants, so representation and wording coverage are not fully separated. Transfer to other tasks and data. Plot comparison remains at 4366% for nearly every adapted model, compared with 52% for the base model. The exception is ftC seed 0, with 72% on nm plots and 65% on eV plots. Specification is absent from training. Its accuracy ranges from 35% to 96% in the four-table arms and falls to 3135% in the nm-only arms, compared with 60% for the base model. On gold, table threshold accuracy drops from 82% to 4981% across ftAc, ftBmc, ftB, and ftC; ftA reaches 7475%. We check whether the adapters have learned to find minimum instead of maximum. Of the 27 adapters, 23 agree with this reversed rule on only 526% of core table requests where the rules differ. The remaining adapters reach 3466%: ftB seed 2, ftC seed 1, and ftCc seeds 0 and 1. common reversal of the rule therefore cannot explain the decline. Converting gold absorbance to transmission = 10A and asking for dip 9 also does not recover transfer (Appendix D). The supplementary arms ftD, ftCc, and ftDc show similar results: plot comparison of 5163%, specification accuracy of 3587%, and gold threshold accuracy of 4881%. Table 11 gives each seed for all 27 adapters.

sections.title: 5.4 Learning to abstain on every truncated input
sections.content: Adapted models reach 88100% table accuracy on the main MOCLIP sufficiency task, compared with 39% for the base model. However, the scope sets show that some gains come from abstaining on any truncated input (Figure 4). Several seeds lose 5470 points on outside cuts, even though only irrelevant samples are removed: ftA seed 2, ftB seed 1, and ftAc seed 0. Longer training on the original labels can worsen this behavior. For nm-only training, mean discrimination falls from +35 in ftA to +18 in ftAc, while the mean outside-cut change falls from 29 to 40. Adding scope instances in ftC gives MOCLIP table discrimination of +96, +94, and +90 across the three seeds. Outside-cut accuracy changes are 0, 0, and 1. There is some transfer to plots despite the absence of images in training: discrimination is +86, +60, and +69. Plot outside-cut changes are less stable, at +12, 8, and 13. On gold tables, ftC discrimination is +70 to +73. This is close to the best earlier seeds, +68 for ftB and +67 for ftBmc, but below low-reasoning Luna at +82. Full-view gold accuracy is only 5267%, compared with 79% for the base model. Also, ftC seed 1 reaches only 0.748 development accuracy and 55% on MOCLIP compare tables, despite its high scope discrimination. Added-data control. ftC adds new examples and increases the number of training updates. To separate these effects, ftD adds 62 instances of the original task types. It has 3,696 training requests, close to ftCs 3,736, and uses the same two-epoch training. All ftD seeds learn the source tasks, reaching 0.991.00 development accuracy and 9899% on MOCLIP compare tables. However, they still abstain too often on answerable truncations. MOCLIP table discrimination is +47, 10, and +12, with outside-cut changes of 27, 98, and 74. On gold tables, ftD matches or exceeds ftC: discrimination is +58 to +78, outside-cut changes are 0 to +8, and full-view accuracy is 5170%. Adding answerable-truncation examples therefore gives more consistent MOCLIP scope performance in these runs. On gold, similar amount of original-task data gives comparable scope behavior. Training to the selected epoch. With ftCs data and the selected-epoch rule, ftCc stops at epochs 2, 2, and 5. Development accuracy is 0.991.00, and MOCLIP compare-table accuracy is 96100%, resolving the undertraining seen in ftC seed 1. Scope performance also remains good. MOCLIP table discrimination is +95, +90, and +100, with outside-cut changes of +2, 2, and 0. Plot discrimination is lower than in ftC, at +56 to +64, while gold table discrimination ranges from +67 to +97. The matched control ftDc uses the same training rule on ftDs data and still varies by seed. MOCLIP table discrimination is 9, +53, and +77, with outside-cut changes of 99, 35, and 0. Plot discrimination is 5 to +42. Across both training durations, all six seeds trained with answerable truncations avoid the shortcut. Five of the six seeds trained with similar amount of original-task data lose 2799 points on outside cuts. On gold tables, the converged arms again give similar results: +67 to +97 for ftCc and +70 to +75 for ftDc.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: Coordinate interpretation. Most models change little when only the wavelength number format changes. Energy coordinates cause larger differences. Asking directly about photon energy helps some models and hurts others on the same evidence. Jevs below-chance result on gold eV tables suggests systematic direction error. To assess this behavior, accuracy and paired representation differences need to be considered together with controls where the correct answer changes. Agreement alone adds little because it largely follows accuracy. Evidence needed for the question. Removing samples outside the query interval leaves the answer available. Removing the relevant extremum does not. Unadapted models often answer both, while some adapted models abstain on both. high abstention rate on unanswerable deletions alone cannot distinguish these behaviors. Similar problems have been reported in retrieval-augmented question answering [1, 11]. In our experiments, answerable truncations remove the shortcut in every training seed. similar amount of extra original-task data, with or without longer training, does so in only one of six seeds. Limited transfer after adaptation. LoRA improves comparison on table representations included in training. Adding answerable truncations also improves scope behavior on the source dataset, with some transfer to plots. Plot comparison remains weak, performance on an unseen task varies widely, and accuracy on second optical dataset falls. These gains are limited to the tested templates, representations, and data. They do not establish that the model has learned general physical rule.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: Both datasets cover narrow range of optical systems, and we select spectra with clear extrema. MOCLIPs 10 nm sampling does not support claims about narrow resonances. The gold dataset contains repeated nominal recipes across batches, so instance-bootstrap intervals may understate uncertainty for new experimental campaign. The tasks use fixed multiple-choice templates. Each scope set has two query intervals, and their boundaries are partly associated with answer bands. We vary plot style, noise, and phrasing only through the stated controls. Only sufficiency tasks offer an abstention option. The adaptation study uses one base model, frozen vision tower, and three seeds per arm. The arms differ in training updates, and two epochs leave ftC seed 1 under-trained. The supplementary and original arms also use different GPUs, so hardware differs in the ftDftC comparison. We cannot verify whether service routes share the same internal model, and we did not evaluate the native OpenAI decision endpoint. API models may change over time, and local runs use different GPUs across rounds. The study developed through sequential pilots and controls; all comparisons are exploratory.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: For the tested models, equivalent optical data often lead to different decisions, and removing required evidence seldom leads to abstention. Paired representation tests show errors that average accuracy can hide. Testing both answerable and unanswerable partial spectra also reveals whether model abstains simply because data are missing. Task-specific adaptation improves the cases covered by training, but transfer to other representations, tasks, and optical data remains limited. Data and code availability. The measurements are available from Figshare [22] and Zenodo [12] under CC BY 4.0. The task definitions, per-response results, training-log summaries and script that regenerates all result tables and figures are available at https://github.com/zwang-devv/spectra-decision-audit. The rendering and model-calling code, raw model outputs and adapter weights are available from the authors on request. Ethics statement. The study uses public, licensed physical measurements and involves no human subjects or personal data. Declarations. Funding: this work received no funding. Competing interests: the authors declare none. Author contributions: Z.W. designed and conducted the study and wrote the manuscript; G.Z. and X.C. contributed ideas and reviewed the manuscript.

sections.title: A Task and execution details
sections.content: MOCLIP band labels are 450605, 605645, 645685 and 685730 nm, with boundaries between sampled wavelengths. Specification windows are 605665, 625685 and 645705 nm; positive candidates lie at least 15 nm inside their window and location distractors at least 30 nm outside; positive and location-distractor dips are at least 0.05 below the depth threshold and shallow distractors at least 0.10 above it. Main MOCLIP contains 96 extreme, 384 compare (192 energy-worded), 144 specification and 96 sufficiency variants; main gold contains 80 threshold (40 energy-worded), 128 compare (64 energy-worded) and 36 sufficiency variants. Jev therefore receives 2,304 MOCLIP and 664 gold main requests, multimodal models 3,552 and 1,048. Dataset generation seeds are 2 (MOCLIP main), 3 (gold main), 5 and 6 (scope sets), and 10, 11 and 12 for the three training pools. LoRA targets are q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, in_proj_qkv, in_proj_z, out_proj, gate_proj, up_proj and down_proj (15,630,336 trainable parameters). Development assignment uses the SHA256 of the instance identifier modulo 1,000 (values below 100). Sample-matched arms draw 632 requests without replacement using the optimization seed. No model is selected by test score. Main d3-nano inference ran on an RTX 2000 Ada and the original training rounds on L4 GPUs; the supplementary batch (Appendix E) ran on an A40. For each model, task and representation the last successful response is used; requests that failed and were retried count once.

sections.title: D Gold transmission view
sections.content: In an auxiliary set, we use the same gold instances but convert background-subtracted absorbance to = 10A and ask for the deepest transmission dip. The extremum wavelength is unchanged. The vertical scale, precision, curve shape, and wording all change together. On core table requests, base d3-nano threshold accuracy is 81%, compared with 82% for absorbance. ftA seeds reach 68/80/78%, ftBm reaches 65/50/82%, and ftB reaches 52/47/71%. Compare accuracy is 46% for the base model, 52/50/52% for ftA, 52/54/40% for ftBm, and 56/50/44% for ftB. Using dip wording, as in the source task, does not recover transfer to gold. We did not evaluate later arms on this view.

sections.title: E Supplementary batch
sections.content: On 24 October 2026, we added the eV row-order control, the Qwen3.5-2B base reference, and further LoRA arms. The protocol was written before these results were seen. We kept earlier task files, responses, and adapters unchanged and made all comparisons for these analyses within the supplementary batch. Row order. The descending-energy table has the same values, wording and options as the original eV table. Every variant that admits an eV table was run in both orders for d3-nano, the Qwen3.5-2B base model, Jev and the three Luna configurations; the oracle is correct on all of them. Same-day ascending reruns reproduced the earlier choices for 99.099.6% of d3-nano requests (on different GPU hardware), 98.8100% for Luna Decisions, 9498% for Jev, 9396% for low-reasoning Luna and 8195% for Luna gen. none; accuracies changed by at most two points. Base-model readout. The base model receives the evidence text, the question, lettered options, and the instruction in Appendix B, using its chat template with thinking disabled. For image requests, the image precedes the text. We choose the option letter with the highest next-token logit and calculate softmax over option letters only. On average, these letters carry 97% of the full next-token probability on MOCLIP and 99% on gold. Additional LoRA arms. The ftD pool adds 6 extreme, 16 compare, and 9 full-range sufficiency instances per polarization, using seed 12. The structure rule is the same as for ftC: additions must be disjoint from every MOCLIP test set but can reuse original training structures. With four table representations, ftD has 3,696 training and 512 development requests, compared with 3,736 and 456 for ftC. ftD, ftCc, and ftDc use the original hyperparameters. The selected epochs are 2, 2, and 5 for ftCc and 9, 2, and 9 for ftDc. Every supplementary adapter reaches development accuracy of 0.991.00. The protocol gives priority in the order ftD > ftCc > ftDc and allows ftDc to be dropped if projected GPU cost exceeds the budget. We initially skipped ftDc based on nine-epoch estimate, then ran it when early stopping reduced the estimate. All three seeds are reported. duplicate ftDc seed-2 job was stopped before completing an epoch; the evaluated adapter comes from the stored run. The batch used about 9.3 GPU-hours and $0.81 in API calls.
